generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology this shows up in the habits the discipline lives by: which questions count as empirical, how evidence from an experiment or a case study is weighed, and how ethical limits shape what you may even ask. Early on much of this is unspoken, picked up from how your lecturers reason about studies and what your reading treats as sound method rather than from anything set out plainly. Noticing those habits, and trying them in your own practical reports and seminar arguments, is how you start to take part in psychology rather than just revise it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two psychology students preparing for the same seminar on the same journal article.

Tom reads the article once and highlights the findings, ready to repeat them if asked. The study has been covered and the results are in his notes. This is surface learning: the information has been taken in, but it sits on its own, and he treats the paper as a set of facts to recall.

Amara reads the same article and keeps asking why. Why did the authors choose this design? How does the sample limit what the findings can claim? Where would a different theory predict something else? By the seminar, Amara can connect the study to a wider debate about method and evidence, and take a reasoned position within it. This is deep learning: the ideas are linked into understanding she can use and defend.

Both students have read the article. Only Amara has taken the step psychology's discourse community values, turning reported findings into a judgement about how good the evidence is.
generatedProse.summary: Learning in psychology means joining a discourse community that makes, tests and argues about evidence together, ethically and by shared methods. You can now identify what makes that different from recalling findings, and begin to recognise the community your own modules draw on. The move from surface to deep learning, and the habits that support it, will matter in every lesson that follows and in your first practical report.

check.body: Which of these would best help you recognise the discourse community of psychology?

items.text: Noticing who produces and debates the key studies, and how they argue from evidence and method.
Counting how many studies your textbook cites, and tallying which topics come up the most often.
Learning the timetable for your lab sessions, and working out which rooms across campus they run in.
Memorising the names of the researchers, and the years their best-known studies were published.

feedback.correct: That's right. You recognise psychology's discourse community by seeing who makes its knowledge and how they reason from evidence and method, not by counting studies or learning logistics.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about how knowledge is made and argued from evidence, rather than counts or logistics.
feedback.incorrectFinal: You recognise psychology's discourse community by noticing who produces and debates its key studies, and how they argue from evidence and method. The other options are about quantity or logistics, not how the community makes knowledge.
